name: Peg-MGF (mechano growth factor)

card.summary: A pegylated synthetic version of the IGF-1Ec peptide sold as a research chemical for muscle growth; human evidence is absent and it is WADA-banned.
card.note: Not approved for any use; WADA-prohibited; research raises carcinogenicity questions.

quick.overview:
Mechano growth factor (MGF, or IGF-1Ec) is a 24-amino-acid peptide the body produces by splicing of the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise. Peg-MGF is a synthetic, pegylated version sold online as a research chemical and used by some bodybuilders for muscle gain.

The published evidence is laboratory and animal work. Reference sources report no human clinical trial results for MGF as a muscle-building drug.
quick.mechanism: Natural MGF is described as acting in muscle repair and is rapidly degraded in the body. Pegylation and amino-acid substitutions in synthetic versions are intended to improve stability.
quick.risks: Not approved as a medicine anywhere. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits MGF. A 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity, and human safety data are not available.

lead: Peg-MGF is a pegylated synthetic version of mechano growth factor (MGF), a short peptide that muscle tissue makes from the IGF-1 gene after training or damage. Bodybuilders discuss it as a way to push muscle growth and recovery after hard sessions, with the aim of a fuller, more muscular physique.[1][2]

MGF (also called IGF-1Ec) was named because its transcript appears in muscle after mechanical loading or injury. Researchers describe it as activating satellite cells, the stem cells that donate nuclei to muscle fibres for repair and hypertrophy, and some reviews call it a local repair factor as well as a growth factor.[2][3][4] Peg-MGF is a research-chemical form that adds polyethylene glycol to lengthen the short life of the natural peptide.[1]

Published work on MGF is laboratory, animal and exercise-physiology research, including human muscle-biopsy studies of how its expression changes after resistance exercise. It is not approved as a medicine, and the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it.[1][1]

chain: Peptide mimics the muscle-repair splice form of IGF-1
Claimed to activate satellite cells after training
angle.text: Users say Peg-MGF supports satellite-cell activation and recovery after lifting, which they hope translates into more muscle size over time. It is discussed alongside growth hormone and IGF-1 in bodybuilding circles.

paras: The IGF-1 gene gives rise to several splice variants. A 2002 review notes that one transcript is detectable only after injury or mechanical activity, giving it the name mechano growth factor; because of a reading-frame shift its sequence and mode of action differ from liver-derived systemic IGF-1.[2] The same review suggests MGF may be regulated as a local repair factor.[2]

A 2010 review describes MGF expression rising in muscle, bone and tendon after mechanical damage and in brain and heart after ischemia, and reports that it has been shown to activate satellite cells, resulting in hypertrophy or regeneration, while noting that its functional mechanism is not well understood.[3]

Reviews report that older muscle responds less to loading: one describes elderly muscle as unable to upregulate MGF after exercise, and another states that short-term high-resistance exercise increased MGF mRNA in young but not elderly subjects.[4][5] A 2004 review reports that GH treatment combined with resistance exercise shifted splicing toward MGF in older people, and discusses the decline of MGF production with age alongside falling growth hormone.[6]
Human studies measure expression in biopsies rather than giving the peptide: they track IGF-1 splice variants after resistance exercise, ultrasound or other stimuli.[7][8]

Natural MGF is broken down rapidly. Wikipedia reports that synthetic versions often use D-amino acids in the central region for stability and that in some products the tyrosine is pegylated.[1] Pegylation is the attachment of polyethylene glycol chains intended to prolong how long a peptide remains in circulation.

No studies found of Peg-MGF given to people. Human research on natural MGF has measured its expression in muscle after exercise or other stimuli.[5][7][8] Laboratory and animal work covers muscle repair, neuroprotection, cardiac protection and muscular dystrophy models.[1][3] A registered trial of pegylated somatropin in short-stature children concerns a different product.[9]

T Nation forum threads from the 2000s mention MGF alongside growth hormone, IGF-1 and steroids as part of long enhancement protocols, with posters citing its effect on satellite cells.[10][11][12] The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits MGF, and doping-control detection methods have been published.[1]
MGF is not approved for any use, and no human safety data for Peg-MGF are published. A 2020 review cited by Wikipedia raised concern about possible carcinogenicity of MGF.[1]

timeline.event: Goldspink publishes a review on muscle response to stretch and overload, an early source in the MGF literature.[1]
Review describes the IGF-1 isoform detectable only after injury or mechanical activity and names it MGF.[2]
Review of IGF-1Ec expression and function across tissues.[3]
A review raises concerns about MGF's potential carcinogenicity.[1]

lore.intro: Peg-MGF appears in muscle-building forum discussions as a localised growth peptide used alongside other anabolic compounds.[10][11]

claims.claim: Peg-MGF activates satellite cells and drives muscle growth after training
claims.believers: Posters say MGF's effect on satellite cells makes it a useful addition to long enhancement protocols.[10]
claims.experts: Reviews report that natural MGF activates satellite cells in lab and animal work, and that its mechanism is poorly understood; no human trials of Peg-MGF are published.[3][4]

claims.claim: Pegylation keeps MGF active long enough to matter
claims.believers: Sellers and users argue that pegylation extends the short half-life of natural MGF.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports natural MGF is rapidly metabolised and that synthetic forms use stabilising modifications; no human pharmacology data are cited.[1]
